item.title: Generative AI: how it works and when to use it

item.content:
A spam filter decides whether an email belongs in the spam folder. A generative model can draft a reply to that email. Both can use machine learning, but they produce different kinds of results.

Generative AI refers to systems that use learned patterns to produce content such as text, code, images, audio or video. The model learns something about how data is structured, then uses that learned structure to generate an output.1

That output can be useful without being correct. It can also resemble training material. “Generated” does not guarantee original, factual or safe to use.

What does “generative” mean?

Think about photographs of cats. A classifier might learn enough to distinguish a cat from a dog. An image generator has a different task: produce an image that fits patterns associated with cats, perhaps conditioned on a request such as “a ginger cat asleep on a blue chair”.

The classifier does not need to draw fur, lighting or a chair to make its decision. The generator needs a way to produce the image.

In statistical terms, a generative model learns a distribution over data, possibly conditioned on inputs. A discriminative classifier learns how inputs relate to labels. The mathematics varies by model family, but the distinction explains why generating a convincing image is different from labeling one.1

These are not mutually exclusive applications. A text generator can also classify an email by producing the word “spam”. A generative model can help solve a prediction task. The label describes its modeling approach, not a rule that forbids other uses.

AI, machine learning, LLMs and agents

These terms describe different things:

Term What it describes
Artificial intelligence The broad field of building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence.
Machine learning Methods that learn patterns or behavior from data rather than relying only on explicit rules.
Deep learning Machine learning with multilayer neural networks. Most prominent current generative systems use it.
Generative AI Systems that use learned models to produce content. Generative modeling also predates today’s deep networks.
Large language model A large model trained on language-related data. Many current LLMs generate text and code.
AI agent An application that selects and performs actions toward a goal, often using an LLM.

A multimodal model handles more than one type of input or output, such as text and images. Check the actual capabilities: accepting an image does not mean a model can generate one.

A model that writes an explanation does not automatically inspect your repository or execute commands. An application has to provide those capabilities. AI agents, skills and the protocols between them covers that application layer.

How does a generative model come to exist?

Someone chooses a model architecture, prepares data and trains the model on an objective. Training changes numerical parameters so the model performs better at that objective.

The broad lifecycle looks like this:

flowchart TD
    A["Choose a task, data sources and permitted uses"] --> B["Prepare and filter training data"]
    B --> C["Train the base model"]
    C --> D["Optional task or instruction training"]
    D --> E["Evaluate quality, safety and limitations"]
    E --> F["Deploy through an application or API"]
    F --> G["Monitor outcomes and evaluate changes"]
    G --> E

Filtering can remove some duplicates, low-quality examples and sensitive information. It cannot certify that everything left is accurate or appropriate. Decide whether the data sources and licenses permit the intended use before training begins.

There is no single training recipe for every generative model. Two examples make that easier to see.

Text: learn to predict the next token

Many text-generating LLMs learn by predicting the next token, which is a piece of text determined by a tokenizer. A token can be a word, part of a word or punctuation.

During training, a passage supplies both the context and the target. For example:

Context: The capital of Kenya is
Target: Nairobi

The actual tokenizer may split “Nairobi” into several tokens. The model predicts a distribution, a loss function measures how its prediction compares with the training target, and an optimizer adjusts the parameters. This happens across many examples.

This is self-supervised learning: the text supplies the prediction targets. It does not mean the entire system develops without human choices or human-generated data.

At inference time, the application gives the trained model a prompt. The model calculates next-token probabilities, a decoding method selects a token, and the process repeats. Parameters normally remain fixed during this process. The GPT-3 paper is one documented example of an autoregressive language model used for many tasks through prompting.2

When decoding samples from those probabilities, the same prompt can produce different answers. Temperature changes how concentrated the sampling distribution is. That affects variation, not whether the answer is factual.3

flowchart TD
    A["Prompt and available context"] --> B["Calculate next-token probabilities"]
    B --> C["Select a token"]
    C --> D["Append it to the sequence"]
    D --> E{"Stop condition reached?"}
    E -->|No| B
    E -->|Yes| F["Return the generated text"]

This explains both the flexibility and a major limitation. Training text contains code, explanations and factual statements, so the model can learn patterns useful for producing them. But the probability of a continuation is not the probability that its claims are true.

For more detail about tokenization, attention and hardware, see Large language models.

Images: learn to remove noise

Diffusion is another approach. In a simplified image diffusion setup, training adds controlled noise to an image and teaches a model to reverse that corruption. Generation starts with noise and repeatedly refines it toward a sample.4

Text-conditioned systems also use a representation of the prompt to guide this process. Some systems work in a compressed representation rather than directly on full-resolution pixels. Diffusion is a family of techniques, not a claim that every image generator follows the same steps.

flowchart LR
    P["Text prompt"] --> C["Conditioning information"]
    N["Initial noise"] --> R["Repeated learned refinement"]
    C --> R
    R --> I["Generated image"]

The text example generates a sequence of tokens. This image example refines a noisy representation. Both are generative, but they do not have the same architecture or inference procedure.

What do instruction tuning and RLHF add?

A base language model trained to continue text is not necessarily good at answering a user’s request. Further training can change that behavior.

Supervised instruction tuning uses examples of requests and desired responses. Preference training uses judgments about which outputs are better. Reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF, is one approach; the InstructGPT paper describes a pipeline with demonstrations, preference judgments and reinforcement learning.5

Post-training can improve behavior, but it does not guarantee truthfulness. Nor does every model use RLHF. “Instruction-tuned” describes a training outcome or method, not proof that a model will reliably obey every instruction.

A foundation model is broadly pretrained so it can be adapted to a range of tasks. The term describes that role, rather than one architecture. Not every generative model has that breadth.6

What is new about it?

Generative modeling did not begin with chatbots. Variational autoencoders were described in work first published in 2013, and generative adversarial networks followed in 2014.78

Model family Basic idea
Autoregressive models Generate a sequence by predicting its next element from preceding elements.
Variational autoencoders Learn a probabilistic latent representation and a decoder that can generate samples.
Generative adversarial networks Train a generator against a discriminator that tries to distinguish generated samples from training examples.
Diffusion models Learn to reverse a corruption process and use that learned process to generate samples.

This table is a map of common approaches, not a complete taxonomy. Architectures and techniques can be combined.

Several developments made modern systems more broadly useful. The Transformer paper introduced an attention-based architecture with more parallelizable training than the recurrent models it compared against.9 Later work such as GPT-3 demonstrated that a large pretrained model could perform varied tasks from instructions and examples in its input, without a separate parameter update for each task.2

Instruction tuning made those capabilities easier to access through conversation. More capable hardware, larger training runs and better serving software helped make the systems available through applications and APIs.

The practical change is that one model can support many tasks through the same language interface. A developer can ask it to summarize an incident, suggest tests or rewrite a function without building a separate specialized model for each request.

That flexibility is useful. It is also why a chatbot demo tells you less than you might expect about whether the same model will handle your production task reliably.

What is the alternative?

The alternative depends on the job. “Use AI” is not a requirement unless the problem actually needs it.

Job A reasonable starting point
Calculate an invoice total Ordinary code with explicit arithmetic and rounding rules.
Return an order’s delivery status A database query or API call.
Classify thousands of messages into known categories A classifier, with comparison against an LLM baseline if useful.
Find an exact clause in a policy Search and show the source passage.
Produce a standard notification A template populated with verified fields.
Draft a custom explanation from several documents A generative model with relevant source material and review.

Traditional software can generate text too. A receipt template produces text, but that does not make it generative AI. The distinction is the learned model, not the mere existence of an output.

Generative AI is a reasonable choice when you need flexible language or content generation and can check the result. It is a poor replacement for an authoritative database or a calculation you already know how to implement.

Often the best application combines both. Fetch the actual order status using code, then let a model help explain it. Do not ask the model to invent the status.

Prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning solve different problems

These terms get mixed together, even though they change different parts of the system.

Technique What changes? Example
Prompting The instructions and context provided for a request. Ask for a short explanation and supply a sample of the desired format.
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG The application retrieves external material and supplies it to the generator. Retrieve the current refund policy before answering a customer.
Fine-tuning Further training updates model parameters or trained adapters. Train for a recurring task or response behavior using curated examples.

RAG combines retrieval with generation. The original RAG paper describes a system that combines a pretrained generator with a retrieval component.10 In a common application, the flow is:

flowchart TD
    Q["Question about a refund"] --> S["Search approved policy documents"]
    S --> P["Relevant passages and source identifiers"]
    Q --> G["Build the model's input"]
    P --> G
    G --> A["Generate an answer grounded in the passages"]
    A --> V["Check claims and source links"]

Retrieving a document during a request does not, by itself, retrain the generator. A conversation stored by an application is not automatically a change to model weights either.

Many retrieval systems use embeddings, numerical representations that help compare passages by similarity. RAG does not require a vector database, though. Keyword search can retrieve useful context too.

For frequently changing information, retrieval is usually a better first step than trying to bake every new fact into weights. Fine-tuning may help with repeated behavior or a specialized task. Neither technique removes the need to evaluate the result.

What should I watch out for?

NIST’s Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile covers risks including confabulation, privacy, harmful bias, information integrity and intellectual property. Choosing a model is only part of managing them.11

Fluent errors

A model can invent an API, a citation or a reason a test failed. People commonly call this a hallucination. Confident wording does not make the answer more reliable.

Check factual claims against sources. Run generated code and meaningful tests. For generated images, inspect details and suitability for the intended use.

Lowering temperature changes generation behavior; it does not switch on a truth mode. Structured output can make a response easier to parse, but valid JSON can still contain a wrong answer.

Performance also varies with the people, languages and situations represented in training and evaluation. A support assistant that handles English examples well may still fail on the languages your customers actually use. Test those cases and check for harmful stereotypes rather than relying on an aggregate score.

Privacy, retention and rights

Before sending documents to a service, check what the provider stores, how long it keeps the data and whether the applicable product terms allow training on it. Do not assume every product from the same provider has the same policy.

Local inference can keep model inputs on your machine, but the surrounding application may still use remote services or telemetry. Check the whole data path.

Keep track of licenses and source provenance when using data or generated material. A model’s ability to produce something does not establish your right to publish it. Requirements also depend on jurisdiction and use.

Untrusted input and real actions

An instruction hidden in a retrieved document can try to redirect an assistant. This is prompt injection. It becomes especially dangerous when the application can send messages, access private information or modify systems.

Treat external material as data, enforce permissions in software and require review for consequential actions. Telling a model to “be careful” is not an access-control mechanism.

Cost, latency and deployment choices

A hosted API reduces the hardware and serving work you manage. Running a model yourself gives you control over more of the stack, but you inherit the operational costs.

Compare the cost of the whole task, including retrieval, long inputs, retries, tool calls and human review. A cheap request that needs several corrections may cost more than a more reliable approach.

Open weights means that model parameters are available under a particular license. It does not necessarily mean the training data, complete training process or unrestricted commercial rights are available. Read the license and model documentation.

How do I know whether it works for my task?

Build a small set of representative examples before choosing a model. Include ordinary requests, ambiguous inputs and cases where the system should decline or ask for help.

For a customer-support assistant, check whether it applies the right policy and cites the passage that supports the answer. Measure unsupported claims as well as successful answers. For code, test behavior rather than whether the explanation sounds convincing.

Compare against a simpler baseline. A search result with a useful excerpt may beat a generated paragraph. Record quality, latency, cost and the consequences of mistakes, then repeat the evaluation when you change the model, prompt or data source.

You do not need to train a foundation model to try this. Start with an existing model, a narrow task and information you are allowed to use. If ordinary code already solves the task clearly, keep it.

References

  1. Google Machine Learning, What is a generative model?. Explains generative and discriminative modeling and why the distinction is about learned distributions. ↩︎ ↩︎

  2. Brown et al. (2020), Language Models are Few-Shot Learners. Documents autoregressive GPT-3 and task examples supplied without parameter updates at inference time. ↩︎ ↩︎

  3. Hugging Face Transformers, Generation strategies. Explains next-token selection, greedy decoding and sampling. ↩︎

  4. Ho, Jain and Abbeel (2020), Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models. A foundational paper on learning and sampling with image diffusion models. ↩︎

  5. Ouyang et al. (2022), Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. Describes the InstructGPT post-training process and remaining limitations. ↩︎

  6. Bommasani et al. (2021), On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models. Defines broadly trained models adaptable to many downstream tasks. ↩︎

  7. Kingma and Welling (first submitted 2013), Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. Introduces the variational autoencoder approach. ↩︎

  8. Goodfellow et al. (2014), Generative Adversarial Networks. Introduces adversarial training of a generator and discriminator. ↩︎

  9. Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need. Introduces the Transformer architecture. ↩︎

  10. Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. Describes generation supported by an external retrieval component. ↩︎

  11. NIST (2024), Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile. A cross-sector guide to generative AI risks and risk-management actions. ↩︎

item.description:
Large language models

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on large amounts of text to learn patterns in language. Those patterns let it generate text, answer questions, translate, write code and summarize documents. Some models also work with images or audio.

item.content:
Large language models

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on large amounts of text to learn patterns in language. Those patterns let it generate text, answer questions, translate, write code and summarize documents. Some models also work with images or audio.

The word model means a mathematical system with learned numerical values, called parameters. Given an input, the system uses those values to calculate an output. “Large” usually refers to the number of parameters and the scale of training; there is no universal size at which a language model becomes an LLM.

It helps to separate the model from the application around it. A chat application can add conversation history, search, file access and tools. The model alone does not automatically have those abilities.

What does it mean to predict text?

For a typical text-generating LLM, prediction means calculating which token could come next, given the tokens already available. A token is a piece of text: a word, part of a word, punctuation or even a space. The tokenizer determines the exact split.

Suppose the input is:

The capital of Kenya is

The model assigns probabilities to possible next tokens. “Nairobi” should be a likely continuation. The application selects a token using a decoding strategy, adds it to the input and repeats the process until it reaches a stopping condition.1

flowchart TD
    A["Prompt text"] --> B["Tokenizer: text to token IDs"]
    B --> C["Model calculates next-token probabilities"]
    C --> D["Decoding strategy selects a token"]
    D --> E["Append token to the sequence"]
    E --> F{"Stop condition reached?"}
    F -->|No| C
    F -->|Yes| G["Decode output tokens into text"]

This is inference: using a trained model. Its parameters normally stay fixed while it generates a response.

Choosing the highest-probability token is one decoding strategy. Sampling is another: it allows different continuations according to their probabilities. A setting called temperature adjusts how concentrated that distribution is. Lower temperatures generally make sampling more predictable; higher ones allow more variation. Neither setting guarantees a correct answer.

Predicting text can produce much more than sentence completion. Training examples contain explanations, programs and worked problems, so the model can learn patterns that support those tasks. But a plausible continuation can still be false. An invented citation or a confident factual error is often called a hallucination. A token’s probability is not the probability that a claim is true.

What is inside a model?

Most widely used LLMs are based on the Transformer, an architecture introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need.2 The following is a simplified view of a decoder-only Transformer, the kind commonly used for text generation.

flowchart TD
    A["Token IDs"] --> B["Token embeddings"]
    B --> C["Position information"]
    C --> D["Causal self-attention: mix information from available tokens"]
    D --> E["Feed-forward network: transform each token representation"]
    E --> F["Repeat Transformer blocks"]
    F --> G["Output layer: scores for vocabulary tokens"]
    G --> H["Convert scores to probabilities"]

The diagram leaves out details such as normalization and residual connections so the main path is easier to follow.

Tokens and embeddings

The tokenizer converts text into numerical IDs. An embedding maps each ID to a vector, which is an ordered list of numbers the network can work with. Position information helps the model distinguish sequences such as “the dog chased the cat” and “the cat chased the dog”.

The initial embedding for a token comes from learned parameters. As the token passes through the model, its representation changes with context. The word “bank” in “river bank” should have a different contextual representation from “bank account”.

You may also encounter embedding models used for search. These produce vectors for whole passages so an application can compare their similarity. They serve a different purpose from a chat model that generates a reply.

Attention and Transformer blocks

Self-attention lets a token’s representation incorporate information from other tokens. In a decoder-only model, causal attention prevents a position from looking ahead at future tokens. For “The keys on the table are missing”, attention can help connect “keys” with “are” despite the words between them.

Each block also has a feed-forward network that transforms the representations. Repeating these blocks lets the model build more complex representations of the sequence.3

The context window is the limit on how many tokens the model can work with in one request. For typical chat models, instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents and generated output all compete for that budget. A large window does not guarantee that the model will use every detail reliably.

Parameters, features and settings

These terms describe different things:

Term What it means
Parameters Values learned during training, including weights in attention, feed-forward and embedding layers. A dense “7B” model has roughly seven billion parameters.
Features Properties represented in the data or inside the network, such as patterns related to syntax or topic. They are often distributed across many activations rather than stored in one named location.
Hyperparameters Choices made about training or architecture, such as learning rate or number of layers.
Generation settings Controls used at inference time, such as temperature and output length. Changing these does not retrain the model.

More parameters can increase capacity, but size alone does not tell you which model will perform best. Training data, architecture and the task also matter.

How does a model learn?

Training changes parameters so the model performs better on an objective. In next-token pre-training, the training text supplies both the input and the correct continuation.

For example, training can use “The capital of Kenya is” as context and the token or tokens for “Nairobi” as targets. The model’s prediction is compared with the actual next token using a loss function. Backpropagation calculates how parameters contributed to the error, and an optimizer adjusts them to reduce the loss. This repeats over many batches of text.

The model can learn a prediction at many positions in a sequence during one training pass. Generating new text is different: in the basic inference loop, each new token depends on the tokens selected before it.

Pre-training and fine-tuning

Pre-training builds the initial model from a broad collection of text, often including code. Data preparation can include deduplication, quality filtering and removal of sensitive material. It cannot guarantee that all errors, bias or private information disappear.

Ordinary next-token pre-training is self-supervised: the targets come from the text itself. People do not need to label every sentence. Explicit demonstrations and preference labels usually enter later, during post-training.3

flowchart TD
    A["Collect and filter text"] --> B["Tokenize text"]
    B --> C["Pre-train on next-token prediction"]
    C --> D["Base model"]
    D --> E["Optional supervised fine-tuning on prompt-response examples"]
    E --> F["Optional preference training"]
    F --> G["Instruction-tuned model"]
    D -.-> H["Evaluate at each stage"]
    E -.-> H
    G -.-> H

This is a common route, not a required recipe for every model.

Fine-tuning is further training of an existing model for a task or behavior. Supervised fine-tuning might use examples of questions paired with useful answers. Preference training uses judgments about which responses are better. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is one approach; the InstructGPT paper documents a pipeline using demonstrations followed by preference-based training.4

Fine-tuning is therefore a form of training, not a separate alternative to it. It starts with learned parameters rather than starting from scratch. Some techniques update the whole model; others train a smaller set of additional parameters, often called adapters.

Prompting and retrieval are different

A prompt changes what the model sees, not its learned parameters. Giving it examples in the prompt is few-shot prompting. Asking without examples is zero-shot prompting. These describe how you use a model, not separate model architectures.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies relevant material from an external source, such as a document index, before the model answers.5 For example, a support application could retrieve the current refund policy and include it with a customer’s question.

flowchart TD
    A["User question"] --> B["Search document index"]
    B --> C["Retrieve relevant passages"]
    A --> D["Build prompt"]
    C --> D
    D --> E["Model generates an answer"]
    E --> F["Answer with source links when supported"]

Retrieval at inference time does not itself retrain the generator. It can provide current facts and source material, but the model can still misread a passage or cite something that does not support its claim.

If you need an answer based on today’s policy, retrieval is usually a better starting point than fine-tuning. If you need consistent output formatting or task behavior, fine-tuning may help.

What kinds of models exist?

There are several ways to describe a model, and the labels overlap.

Architecture

Architecture How it works Examples and common uses
Encoder-only Builds representations using context on both sides of a token. BERT; classification, extraction and search representations.
Decoder-only Uses preceding tokens to predict the next token. GPT and Llama families; chat, code and text generation.
Encoder-decoder Encodes an input, then generates an output conditioned on it. T5; translation and summarization.

BERT is a useful architectural comparison, though people often mean generative decoder-only models when they say “LLM” today.3

Another distinction is dense versus mixture-of-experts (MoE). A dense model uses the same parameter blocks for each token. An MoE model routes tokens through selected expert networks. Its total parameter count can be much larger than the number active for each token, so total size and computation per token are different measurements.

Training, inputs and access

A base model has undergone pre-training. An instruction-tuned model has further training to respond to instructions. A domain-specific model has training focused on an area such as medicine or code. One model can be both instruction-tuned and domain-specific.

A multimodal model accepts or produces more than text, for example images or audio. A text-only model cannot inspect a photograph just because a chat interface allows an attachment.

With open-weight models, you can obtain the learned parameters and run them yourself, subject to the license. That does not necessarily mean the training data or full training process is available. Hosted proprietary models are generally accessed through an application or API instead. Always check the particular model’s license and model card rather than assuming “open” means unrestricted.

What does “frontier” mean?

A frontier model is generally one near the leading edge of capability at a given time. It is not a particular architecture or parameter count, and the label moves as models improve. Policy definitions can be narrower: the paper Frontier AI Regulation focuses on highly capable foundation models that could pose severe risks to public safety.6

For choosing a model, a result on your own task is more useful than the label. A smaller specialist may be sufficient for extracting fields from invoices even if a frontier model performs better on broad benchmarks.

Why does hardware matter?

Running a model means doing large amounts of numerical computation and moving its parameters through memory. Training adds the work of calculating gradients and updating parameters, plus memory for training state.

GPUs perform many operations in parallel and have memory systems suited to these workloads. They were developed for graphics, but the same ability to process large arrays of numbers is useful for neural networks.

High-end AI GPUs are expensive partly because they combine complex chips with large amounts of fast memory and high-speed connections. A training cluster also needs networking, power and cooling. Price depends on supply and demand as well as hardware capability; it is not simply a price per parameter.

GPUs are not mandatory for all inference. CPUs can run smaller models, often at lower speed. Google’s Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) are specialized accelerators for machine-learning workloads, especially large matrix operations.7 Phones and laptops may also have neural processing units (NPUs), but the runtime must support the hardware and model.

Will a model fit on my computer?

A useful first estimate is:

weight memory = parameter count x bits per parameter / 8

For a dense 7B model, that gives:

Weight precision Approximate weight memory
32-bit 28 GB
16-bit 14 GB
8-bit 7 GB
4-bit 3.5 GB

These are decimal gigabytes for the weights alone, not total system requirements. You also need memory for intermediate calculations, runtime overhead and, in typical Transformer generation, a KV cache. This cache stores attention keys and values from processed tokens so the runtime can reuse them. Longer contexts and more simultaneous requests increase its memory use.

Quantization stores weights, and sometimes other values, with fewer bits. It can reduce memory requirements substantially, but quality and speed depend on the method and hardware.8 A 4-bit 7B model therefore needs more than 3.5 GB of usable memory to run.

Local inference also depends on memory bandwidth, supported operations and how quickly you need an answer. Having enough disk space to download a model does not mean you have enough RAM or GPU memory to run it comfortably.

What about phones?

Phones can run smaller models, often with quantization and runtimes designed for the device. Some small models are trained through distillation, where a larger model helps teach a smaller one.

The constraints include shared memory, battery use and heat. A model that runs for a short demonstration may slow down under sustained use. On-device inference can work offline and keep inputs on the device, provided the application does not send them elsewhere. Google’s LiteRT-LM is one runtime for deploying models on mobile and other devices.9

What software connects an application to a model?

The model weights are only part of a working system. A runtime loads them and executes the computation. A server can expose that runtime through an API, which an application calls.

flowchart TD
    A["User"] --> B["Application: UI, history and permissions"]
    B --> C["Local or remote API"]
    C --> D["Inference runtime"]
    E["Model weights and tokenizer"] --> D
    D --> F["CPU, GPU or other supported accelerator"]
    D --> G["Generated response"]
    G --> B

For local use, Ollama manages model downloads and provides an API. llama.cpp runs supported models on CPUs and several GPU backends, including mixed CPU/GPU execution.

For development, Hugging Face Transformers provides model-loading, training and inference APIs. For serving concurrent requests, vLLM provides an inference server with batching and memory-management optimizations. Hosted model APIs move the hardware and serving work to a provider, in exchange for usage charges and the provider’s data-handling terms.

These tools are not interchangeable with the models they run. Check the runtime’s support for the model architecture, file format, quantization method and hardware.

Using models well

LLMs are useful for drafting, summarizing and translating text, extracting structured information and helping with code. The amount of checking depends on the consequences of an error. A draft email and a medical recommendation should not have the same review process.

For a concrete task, compare candidate models on representative examples. Check correctness, latency, memory use, cost and data-handling requirements. For code, run tests. For factual answers, open the cited sources and check that they support the claims. A polished answer is still an answer you may need to verify.

References

The numbered notes link claims to source papers and documentation. The Transformer paper explains the architecture; the Hugging Face course is a more approachable starting point. Runtime links above lead to their own documentation.

  1. Hugging Face, Text generation. A practical guide to token generation and decoding settings. ↩︎

  2. Vaswani et al. (2017), Attention Is All You Need. The original Transformer paper. ↩︎

  3. Hugging Face LLM Course, How do Transformers work?. Covers architecture families, self-supervised learning, pre-training and fine-tuning. ↩︎ ↩︎ ↩︎

  4. Ouyang et al. (2022), Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. Documents supervised fine-tuning and RLHF for InstructGPT. ↩︎

  5. Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks. A foundational paper combining retrieval with generation. ↩︎

  6. Anderljung et al. (2023), Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety. A risk-focused definition of frontier AI. ↩︎

  7. Google Cloud, Introduction to Cloud TPU. Explains TPUs and workload considerations for CPUs, GPUs and TPUs. ↩︎

  8. Hugging Face Transformers, Quantization overview. Describes reduced-precision storage and supported methods. ↩︎

  9. Google AI Edge, LiteRT-LM overview. Documents a runtime for on-device language models and supported accelerators. ↩︎

item.title: AI agents, skills and the protocols between them
item.description:
An assistant that explains a failing test and an assistant that investigates the failure are doing different jobs. The first can answer from the information in a prompt. The second needs to inspect files, run a test, read the result and decide what to try next.

That second case is where agents become useful. But the vocabulary around them gets confusing quickly. An agent, a skill and an MCP server can all appear in the same application without being the same thing.
